cards.title: Test RSAs with 7–9 Headlines, Not Always 15
cards.summary: Start responsive search ads with roughly 7–9 headlines to get faster clickthrough-rate readouts instead of maxing the 15-headline cap.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing responsive search ads for a search campaign and deciding how many headline and description variants to write.
steps: Write 7–9 headline variants covering distinct angles you believe are viable for the product or category, rather than padding to Google's 15-headline maximum.
Add more variants if you genuinely have more viable angles, but do not treat Google's ad strength meter as a reason to fill every slot; ad strength is a separate signal from ad rank.
Let Google rotate them unpinned in most cases; only pin when you have a promotion that must be shown, or a proven high-CTR angle that must always serve.
After a short run, pull headline and description performance, keep the winners, remove the losers, and add a few new angle variants to keep testing.
Review performance on a regular cadence rather than setting copy and revisiting 12 months later, because new competitors enter the auction with new angles.
caveats: The 7–9 figure is the presenter's working heuristic, not a performance benchmark.
Pinning limits Google's testing flexibility, so pin only with a stated reason.

cards.title: Five Ad Assets That Expand Search Real Estate
cards.summary: Use sitelinks, callouts, promotions, price assets and structured snippets to occupy more SERP space and lift CTR at no added media cost.
cards.use_when: Finalizing search ad assets for a campaign and choosing which extensions to add for a product category or store.
steps: Add sitelinks pointing to useful non-homepage destinations: bestsellers, collection pages, new arrivals, promotions/clearance, and a reviews page for social proof.
Add up to 10 callouts of 25 characters each that highlight concrete differentiators (for example battery life or included services) that could tip a click.
Add a promotion asset for live sales or evergreen offers, and optionally repeat the offer in the headline.
Use price assets mainly when you want to show value on low-cost ranges ('starting from') or to disqualify clicks on high-priced or luxury items.
Add structured snippets — styles/categories for most stores, or brands stocked if you are a reseller — to add another scannable line of relevance.
Treat these as a repeated test area: refresh assets as offers and ranges change so the larger ad footprint stays relevant.
caveats: Extension types, character limits and the ad-assets interface change; verify current formats in the account before building.
The source notes price assets are used only occasionally and suit specific cases.

cards.title: Bid Strategy Progression for New vs Existing Accounts
cards.summary: Start new Google Ads accounts on manual bidding to gather conversions, then move to value-based automated bidding once conversion volume supports it.
cards.use_when: Choosing a bid strategy for a new or recently relaunched account, or planning when to switch a store's search campaigns to automated bidding.
steps: In a new account or one without recent conversion history, avoid automated bidding first — machine learning has little data and tends to bid erratically and inflate CPCs.

Choose manual CPC (set a max cost per click per keyword, preferring this roughly 70–80% of the time per the source) or maximize clicks (give a daily budget and let Google buy the most clicks, optionally with a CPC ceiling) to generate conversion data quickly.
Manually review and trim keywords and search terms using that data; the goal is enough conversions to justify automated bidding.
Treat an account as 'existing' only if it has recent conversion history; a paused account returning after a long gap should be treated as new.
For existing accounts, pick maximize conversion value over maximize conversions, because e-commerce orders have different values and the algorithm should weight high-value purchases.
Start new campaigns on maximize conversion value with a daily budget around 3–4x average order value, let it learn, then move to target ROAS at roughly 30–50 conversions per month.
caveats: Conversion thresholds (30/50 per month) are the source's stage heuristics, not calculated rules.
Lead-gen-style fixed-value models suit target CPA; variable-basket stores generally suit target ROAS.

cards.title: Set Target ROAS At or Below Historical Actuals
cards.summary: Set an initial target ROAS at or slightly under recent actual ROAS so the algorithm can spend and learn before you tighten efficiency.
cards.use_when: Moving a store's campaign from maximize conversion value to target ROAS bidding, or when a target-ROAS campaign has stopped spending.
steps: Review actual ROAS over roughly the last 30 days under the current bid pattern before setting any target.
Set the first target ROAS at that actual level or slightly below it (for example ~250% actual, set 220–250%) and hold it for at least 2–3 weeks.
Let the campaign spend and generate data; too-low a target risks blowing through efficiency KPIs, so align it to what the business genuinely needs.
Raise the target gently as you observe improved efficiency, or hold the target and scale through budget if growth is the goal.
If a target-ROAS campaign stops spending or performance collapses, suspect the target is set too far above what the account has actually achieved.
caveats: A very high target does not create efficiency; it usually just stops spend entirely, so this is a constriction risk not a stretch goal.
Target ROAS and target CPA behave relative to the target you set — the ranking or auction does not change to meet it.

cards.title: Check Google Can Read Your Site Before Running DSA
cards.summary: Run your target pages through Keyword Planner to confirm Google interprets the products before spending on dynamic search ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether dynamic search ads are viable for a store, or diagnosing poor DSA relevance.
steps: In an existing account, open Keyword Planner and use the option to get keyword ideas from your site or specific URLs.
Enter the landing pages you plan to target with DSA and review whether returned keywords match the product category intent you actually want.
If Google surfaces branded and category-relevant terms (as in the source's example of a supplement brand returning category terms), DSA can likely work.

If the output is irrelevant or generic, fix page clarity and crawlability before launching DSA, because DSA headlines, keywords and landing page selection all run off Google's interpretation of the site.
caveats: DSA gives Google autonomy over headlines, keywords and landing page choice — you only supply descriptions, assets and ad targets.
Keyword Planner interface options change; confirm the current interface before following these steps.

cards.title: Configure DSA Targets and Negatives by Category
cards.summary: Segment DSA ad groups by product theme and block non-commercial pages to avoid wasted spend on irrelevant queries.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up dynamic search ads for a multi-category store.
steps: Choose your ad targets: all landing pages from standard ad groups, URL-based rules (URL contains a category term), category equals, or specific URLs.
Segment at the ad group level by theme — one DSA ad group per category such as men's shoes, women's shoes, children's shoes — rather than mixing everything in one group.
Add negative ad targets for pages you don't want crawled or served against, such as privacy policy, blog pages and return policy, especially in the initial phase.
Once running, review your search term report frequently and continue adding irrelevant terms as negatives.
Apply the same bidding discipline as RSAs: manual bidding in a new account, then automated once conversions reach roughly 30+ per month per the source's heuristic.
caveats: DSA is best used to expand reach and mine new keywords alongside existing RSAs, not usually as the sole campaign type.
Google's autonomy means the landing page a visitor sees may differ from the one you'd pick.

cards.title: Use DSA as a Test Proxy for Performance Max Search
cards.summary: Test search behavior with DSA before committing budget to Performance Max, since the search component behaves similarly.
cards.use_when: Planning a move into Performance Max or deciding whether to run DSA first for a store.
steps: If already running shopping or video campaigns, add DSA campaigns to generate readouts on how search within Performance Max is likely to perform.
Compare DSA search performance against your existing RSA performance to gauge whether adding Performance Max makes sense.
Use DSA for keyword mining at the same time: it can surface new converting search terms that RSA keyword research misses given the volume of new queries daily.
Feed any strong DSA search terms back as keywords in more tightly controlled campaigns.
caveats: This is the source's analogy, not a guaranteed equivalence — treat DSA results as directional evidence.
Performance Max behavior and interface change often; confirm current capabilities.

cards.title: Decide Whether to Run Branded Search
cards.summary: Run branded search campaigns when competitors bid on your brand or you need early conversion data, and skip them when you already dominate organic with no competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to allocate budget to a branded search campaign for a store.
steps: Run branded search if competitors are bidding on your brand name, or if the account is new and needs easy conversion volume to feed machine learning.
Skip it (per the source, almost always) if there is no competitor bidding and your organic listing reliably shows first for brand queries, since you would just pay for traffic you already get.

If you run it, target exact match brand variations (brand, brand + shoes, brand reviews, brand men's) and map each to a relevant page — reviews page for review queries, collection page for category queries.
Add your brand as phrase match to capture untargeted long-tail brand terms, then promote converting search terms from the search term report into exact match keywords.
Exclude branded terms from all other search campaigns via negative keyword lists or brand exclusions, so non-brand campaigns are measured on genuinely incremental traffic.
caveats: The 'almost always skip' stance is the presenter's opinion and depends on your organic ranking and competitive reality.
Excluding brand from other campaigns matters for interpreting incrementality; not doing so inflates non-brand performance.

cards.title: Branded Search Ad Copy, Bidding and 90% Impression Share
cards.summary: Use manual CPC, pin the brand in headline one and target 90%+ impression share on branded search so competitors cannot take bottom-funnel clicks.
cards.use_when: Setting up copy, bids and targets for a branded search campaign.
steps: Pin headline one to your brand name with an authority framing (for example 'brand official store'), since searchers are already looking for you.
Test multiple headline-two angles — offer, shipping, feature/benefit — but generally pair the brand headline with some form of offer.
Add multiple sitelinks to expand the ad and send users to collection pages, active promotions, bestsellers and a dedicated reviews page for trust.
Bid with manual CPC and aim for over 90% impression share, or use target impression share as an alternative; the source avoids automated bidding on branded campaigns.
Track the cost per conversion — the source expects branded conversions to cost only a couple of dollars — and investigate if it is materially higher.
caveats: The 'over 90% impression share' and 'couple of dollars' figures are the source's targets, not universal benchmarks; they will vary by market and competition.
The advice to never use automated bidding on branded campaigns is a strong presenter preference and should be treated as opinion.

cards.title: Performance Max Basic Setup for Ecommerce
cards.summary: Configure Performance Max for purchase value, exclude your brand and hand it clean assets and first-party signals.
cards.use_when: Launching a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce store.
steps: Create a new campaign, choose Sales, optimize for purchases, select Performance Max and link your Merchant Center account so products are available.
Choose conversion-value focus rather than conversion-count focus, since order values differ across the catalogue.
Leave the target ROAS field blank initially and let the campaign run on maximize conversions for the first 2–4 weeks so the algorithm can learn.

Set location and language, then add a brand exclusion (all brand spellings and misspellings) or a negative keyword list so the campaign does not serve on your own brand where dedicated branded campaigns exist.

Skip Google's AI asset generation and supply your own assets: roughly 6–7 headlines (30 characters each), long headlines (90 characters), and 3–4 descriptions (90 characters), plus images, videos, sitelinks and extensions.

Name each asset group by product theme and segment by theme rather than selecting all products, because centralizing copy, landing pages and creative around one theme is more coherent than letting Google bundle everything.
caveats: Interface layout for campaign creation changes; verify current steps in the account.
The source says more than 15 headlines is unnecessary but that filling slots is optional.

cards.title: Performance Max Budget, Search Themes and Audience Signals
cards.summary: Set a PMax daily budget of at least 3x average CPA and use first-party customer lists as the main signal.
cards.use_when: Sizing budget and configuring signals at Performance Max launch for a store.
steps: Set the average daily budget at least at 3x your non-branded average CPA — for example, a $40 CPA implies a floor of about $120/day.
If the store cannot commit roughly $100/day to Performance Max, prefer running shopping and search campaigns instead of funneling a small budget into PMax.

Add search themes only if you deliberately want to push search hard inside PMax, using proven converting keywords or search terms from the account; otherwise omit them because they can cannibalize traffic from your search campaigns.

Add audience signals using first-party lists — all-time customers, top-value customers, or last-12-months customers — which the source has seen shorten the learning phase compared with leaving it blank or using custom/in-market segments.
caveats: The 3x average CPA budget rule and roughly $100/day minimum are the source's heuristics, not calculated requirements.
The source reports poorer performance when search themes are added throughout their accounts and mixed outside feedback on audience signals — treat both as directional.

cards.title: Performance Max Learning Phase and Bid Progression
cards.summary: Give Performance Max 4–6 weeks and move from maximize conversion value to target ROAS once it reaches about 50 conversions per month.
cards.use_when: Managing an early-stage Performance Max campaign and deciding when to change bid strategy.
steps: Expect a long learning phase for Performance Max — sometimes 4–6 weeks — and avoid frequent structural changes that prolong it.
Start on maximize conversion value and review whether the campaign reaches roughly 50 conversions per month inside a single campaign.
At that point transition to target ROAS and set the target at or slightly below the campaign's actual ROAS so the algorithm keeps room to spend.
Then either scale by raising spend while holding the target, or gently raise the target ROAS as efficiency improves.
Review campaign structure changes only after the learning phase has settled.
caveats: The 50-conversions-per-month threshold is the source's heuristic and should be tested against your own campaign volume.
Setting target ROAS far above actual performance typically strangles spend rather than improving efficiency.

cards.title: Ongoing Performance Max Optimization Checklist
cards.summary: Review search terms, negatives, channel mix, audiences and assets on a regular cadence because PMax is not set-and-forget.
cards.use_when: Running weekly or monthly optimization on a Performance Max campaign for a store.
steps: Review search term reports (and search categories) for irrelevant terms and add negatives; in new accounts or new campaigns check every 48–72 hours.
Check brand exclusions are in place for both your own brand and, if desired, competitor brands, keeping brand and non-brand traffic cleanly separated for honest performance measurement.

Review channel/new PMax reporting to see impressions, interactions, spend and purchase value by network — search vs shopping vs video — and use a script like the one credited to Mike Rose for asset-group level cost and top-product detail if in-platform reporting is incomplete.

Inspect audience segments for demographic and in-market skew (the source cites an example of 5x more clicks from one age band) and use those findings to build custom segments for this or other campaigns.
Review asset performance (headlines, descriptions), remove persistently poor performers and add fresh angles to test on a recurring basis.
caveats: Micro-script and channel reporting availability varies by account and UI state; verify current reporting before relying on it.
Asset performance labels are Google's representations, not ground-truth conversion measures.

cards.title: Choose One or Two Performance Max Campaigns Over Sprawl
cards.summary: Consolidate PMax into one campaign with themed asset groups until budget allocation clearly justifies splitting out a scaling campaign.
cards.use_when: Structuring a store's Performance Max campaigns when deciding between consolidation and segmentation.
steps: When running significant shopping and manual search alongside PMax, consolidate into one PMax campaign with asset groups separated by theme (bestsellers, category two, category three).

If a theme — for example bestsellers — is not getting adequate budget, extract it into a second, scaling-focused PMax campaign with a more aggressive target aimed at known bestsellers and top converters.
Keep the remaining adjunctive categories in the efficiency-focused campaign.

Reach for consolidation first; the source notes most brands in the roughly $100k–500k/month Google Ads range still benefit most from consolidated structure, with segmentation becoming more worthwhile above that level and only in certain cases.
caveats: The $100k–500k per month range is the source's observation of its client base, not a formula.
Even above that level, the source says there are cases where segmentation is better — do not treat consolidation as an absolute rule.

cards.title: Demand Gen for Remarketing to Cart Abandoners
cards.summary: Build remarketing with Demand Gen rather than Display, optimizing for purchases and targeting cart abandoners.
cards.use_when: Setting up a remarketing campaign to recover abandoned carts for an ecommerce store.
steps: Go to ads.google.com, open campaigns, create a new campaign, choose sales as the objective and purchases as the conversion focus.
Select Demand Gen as the campaign type, which serves image and video ads across YouTube, Discover, Gmail and the display network, so you can reach returning visitors without relying on display alone.
For the starter campaign in the source's example, target cart abandoners so the ads speak directly to people who reached the cart but did not complete a purchase.
Serve dynamic remarketing creative so the ads reference the products the visitor viewed.
Use Demand Gen for remarketing before display; the source reports Demand Gen far outperforming display for remarketing across its accounts.
caveats: The source's remarketing example is described as a setup demonstration — no specific conversion lift figures are given, so avoid assuming results.
Demand Gen placement and campaign creation options change frequently; verify the current interface.
